title_key: responsible digital technology adoption in nigerian secondary stem education a rights religious pluralism and child safeguarding framework|ukule
title: Responsible Digital Technology Adoption in Nigerian Secondary STEM Education: A Rights, Religious-Pluralism and Child-Safeguarding Framework
abstract: Digital platforms, learning analytics and generative artificial intelligence may widen access to STEM resources, support teachers and enable new forms of inquiry. They may also collect children's data, mediate speech and belief, amplify bias, expose learners to harm or displace accountable human judgment. This normative policy review examines responsible adoption in Nigerian secondary STEM education through constitutional rights, child-rights standards, data-protection law, education policy and international ethical guidance. It proposes the RIGHTS framework: Rights and best interests; Inclusion and equitable access; Governance of data and vendors; Human agency and pedagogical purpose; Trust, transparency and contestability; and Safeguarding across the technology lifecycle. Religious pluralism is treated as a rights and professional-practice issue: public education should neither impose nor disparage belief, and digital systems should support age-appropriate inquiry without profiling, stereotyping or coercion. The framework specifies a pre-procurement assessment, proportionate data controls, accessibility and offline alternatives, human review of consequential outputs, reporting and remedy pathways, and periodic exit decisions. It is a legal-ethical and policy synthesis, not legal advice, an empirical survey or a theological adjudication. Nigerian schools and authorities should obtain competent legal and safeguarding review for particular deployments. Responsible innovation is defined not by tool novelty but by demonstrated educational value, lawful and minimal data use, child participation, pluralism, safety and accountable human control.

title_key: effectiveness of intelligent educational platforms in teaching programming|urozboyev
title: EFFECTIVENESS OF INTELLIGENT EDUCATIONAL PLATFORMS IN TEACHING PROGRAMMING
abstract: This article examines the effectiveness of intelligent educational platforms used in teaching programming. Existing platforms such as Codecademy, LeetCode, PyTutor, ITS-CAL, Codio, and GitHub Copilot are analyzed, and their impact on the educational process is evaluated based on international research. Systematic literature review and meta-analysis methods were employed. The results demonstrate that intelligent platforms positively influence students' knowledge levels, motivation, and independent learning skills, while also revealing challenges such as over-dependence and decreased critical thinking abilities. The article also addresses the current state of digital educational technology implementation in Uzbekistan's higher education institutions and provides a local contextual analysis.

title_key: pengaruh vibe coding berbasis kecerdasan buatan terhadap kompetensi pemrograman mahasiswa di era digital|sinata
title: PENGARUH VIBE CODING BERBASIS KECERDASAN BUATAN TERHADAP KOMPETENSI PEMROGRAMAN MAHASISWA DI ERA DIGITAL
abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has given rise to a new approach in software development known as Vibe Coding. This approach enables programmers to generate source code through natural language instructions with the assistance of generative AI models. This study aims to analyze the influence of AI-based Vibe Coding on students' programming competencies in the digital era. The research employed a quantitative approach using a survey design involving 30 Informatics students who had experience using AI coding assistant platforms. Data were collected through questionnaires and analyzed using simple linear regression. The findings indicate that the use of Vibe Coding has a positive and significant effect on improving students' programming competencies. Vibe Coding assists students in understanding programming syntax, accelerating the debugging process, enhancing software development productivity, and encouraging the exploration of emerging technologies. However, excessive reliance on Vibe Coding may potentially reduce students' algorithmic thinking and independent problem-solving abilities. Therefore, it is essential to implement learning strategies that balance the utilization of AI tools with a strong understanding of fundamental programming concepts.Keywords: Vibe Coding, Artificial Intelligence, Programming Competency, Students, Digital Era.

title_key: exploring the awareness and utilization of chatgpt artificial intelligence by academic staff for enhancing job performance in colleges of education in delta state|ezugoh
title: EXPLORING THE AWARENESS AND UTILIZATION OF CHATGPT ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE BY ACADEMIC STAFF FOR ENHANCING JOB PERFORMANCE IN COLLEGES OF EDUCATION IN DELTA STATE
abstract: The laxity and poor job performance of many academic staff in Colleges of Education (COEs) in Delta State which has become worrisome especially in this digitalized era, necessitated this present study. This study explored the awareness and utilization of ChatGPT Artificial Intelligence (AI) by academic staff for enhancing their job performance in COEs in Delta State. The purpose of this study was to determine the level of awareness, percentage level of utilization and current pattern of ChatGPT (AI) usage among academic staff in Delta State COEs. As such, three research questions guided this study. A descriptive survey research design was adopted in the study. Population for the study constituted 729academic staff from two colleges of education (COE)in Delta State. The sample size for the study comprised a total of 365 academic staff selected at 50% from their entire population using proportionate stratified random sampling technique. A research instrument constructed by the researchers and titled: “Exploring Awareness and Utilization of ChatGPT Artificial Intelligence (AI) for Enhancing Academic Staff Job Performance Questionnaire (EAUCGPTAIEASJPQ)” containing 33 items was used for data collection. The questionnaire was structured on different rating scales. Both validity and reliability of the questionnaire were established. Data collated were analyzed using mean statistics rated at 2.50 and standard deviation. Findings of the study indicated among others that; the academic staff were only aware of ChatGPT (AI) in certain areas, but were not aware of ChatGPT (AI) in majority of the areas investigated in order to enhance their job performance in the COEs in Delta State. They did not also utilize ChatGPT for enhancing their job performance in the COEs. The study recommended among others that the college management in collaboration with the National Commission for Colleges of Education (NCCE) and financial assistance from the Federal and State governments, should prioritize comprehensive training programmes and on-going professional development through workshops, seminars, online courses and hands-on sessions to familiarize academic staff with ChatGPT AI practical applications in educational context and create awareness to them concerning the importance of exploring this new technology for enhancing their job performance and building their capacity for effective utilization.
venue: Scientific Journal of Educational Management, Research and law

title_key: artificial intelligence in teacher training programs a short study|jahan
title: Artificial Intelligence in Teacher Training Programs: A Short Study
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape of teacher education. This article systematically reviews research published between 2015 and 2025 on the application of AI in pre-service and in-service teacher training programs. It analyzes the types of AI applications, their effectiveness, implementation challenges, and best practices. The review finds that AI is used in intelligent feedback systems, adaptive learning platforms, generative AI for lesson planning, and virtual simulations. AI significantly improves teachers’ instructional design skills, technology integration abilities, reflective practices, and AI literacy. However, challenges such as low teacher motivation, training content disconnected from real classrooms, and ethical and privacy concerns remain prominent. Effective AI teacher training should be teacher-centered, hands-on, ethics-oriented, and deeply integrated with authentic teaching contexts. This article provides evidence-based recommendations for educational institutions and policymakers to build sustainable and effective AI-enhanced teacher training systems.
venue: JOURNAL OF ADVANCE AND FUTURE RESEARCH

title_key: the effect of ai powered writing assistants on essay writing performance among students of lagos state college of health technology yaba lagos state|dawodu
title: THE EFFECT OF AI-POWERED WRITING ASSISTANTS ON ESSAY WRITING PERFORMANCE AMONG STUDENTS OF LAGOS STATE COLLEGE OF HEALTH TECHNOLOGY, YABA, LAGOS STATE
abstract: This study investigated the effect of AI-powered writing assistants on the essay writing performance of students of the Lagos State College of Health Technology, Yaba, Lagos State. The rapid spread of tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and QuillBot has transformed how students draft, revise, and refine written work, yet empirical evidence on their effect within Nigerian health-technology colleges remains limited. The study was guided by three objectives, three research questions, and three hypotheses. A quasiexperimental design complemented by a survey was adopted, and data were collected from a sample of 200 students drawn from the College using a structured instrument, the AI Writing Assistant and Essay Performance Questionnaire (AIWEPQ), together with pre-test and post-test essay scores rated with a standardized rubric. Research questions were answered using performance percentage analysis and descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation, while the hypotheses were tested using Pearson product-moment correlation and multiple linear regression at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that the use of AI-powered writing assistants was widespread and was associated with marked improvements in grammar and mechanics, coherence and organization, and vocabulary and style. Mean essay scores in the AI-assisted (experimental) group rose from 48.6% at pre-test to 68.9% at post-test, compared with a smaller rise from 49.1% to 54.3% in the control group. A strong, positive, and significant relationship was found between the use of AI writing assistants and essay writing performance (r = 0.71, p < 0.05), and the regression model showed that three dimensions of AI assistance jointly explained about 55% of the variance in performance (R² = 0.55, p < 0.05), with grammar and feedback support the strongest predictor. The study concluded that AI-powered writing assistants significantly enhance essay writing performance when used responsibly, and it recommended guided integration, training, and safeguards for academic integrity

title_key: as a teacher imagines developing english educational apps with vibe coding|society
title: As a teacher imagines: Developing English educational apps with vibe coding
abstract: This study explores the potential of “vibe coding,” an AI-assisted, no-code development method, to empower pre-service elementary school teachers to design and implement English educational apps. The study was conducted with 53 participants from a university of education who were provided guided training using ChatGPT and Qwen to develop HTML-based educational apps. Participants designed apps incorporating diverse language skills, such as vocabulary, listening, and writing, as well as gamification and digital scaffolding techniques. The results showed that non-programmers could effectively develop functional apps using natural language prompts and that their theoretical understanding of English education significantly influenced the quality of their educational outputs. Survey responses further revealed that participants recognized the importance of AI and digital literacy as key competencies for future teachers. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the strong pedagogical potential of vibe coding in fostering teacher agency, creativity, and adaptive expertise in technology-integrated education.

title_key: dampak tantangan dan potensi vibe coding berbasis ai dalam lanskap pendidikan pemrograman tinjauan literatur sistematis|purnajaya
title: Dampak Tantangan dan Potensi Vibe Coding Berbasis AI dalam Lanskap Pendidikan Pemrograman: Tinjauan Literatur Sistematis
abstract: Vibe coding transforms natural language commands into functional code through Artificial Intelligence (AI). This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) evaluates the impacts, challenges, and potential of this approach within education. Adhering to the PRISMA protocol, 17 studies were selected based on inclusion criteria. The distribution encompasses higher education (n=9) and K-12 (n=8), focusing on tools like GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT. Synthesis results from controlled experimental studies among higher education students indicate a significant increase in task completion efficiency of up to 35%. However, a distinction is observed where increased technical productivity does not equate to improved learning achievement; instead, risks concerning diminished conceptual understanding and academic integrity challenges remain. This review is limited by the geographic dominance of studies from North America and Europe and the high heterogeneity of study designs, which necessitated a narrative synthesis. This study recommends a pedagogical shift towards critical human-AI collaboration.
venue: Jurnal Teknologi informasi dan Ilmu Komputer

title_key: academic integrity in the age of artificial intelligence examining the effect of ai integration on learning research productivity and ethical standards of business and accountancy students as future industry professionals|velasco
title: Academic Integrity in The Age of Artificial Intelligence: Examining the Effect of AI Integration on Learning, Research Productivity, And Ethical Standards of Business and Accountancy Students as Future Industry Professionals
abstract: Abstract — Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, including ChatGPT, Grammarly, and QuillBot, are increasingly integrated into academic work, reshaping how students approach research, writing, and ethical decision-making. While previous studies have examined AI adoption in education from a pedagogical perspective, there is limited research connecting AI use to management-relevant constructs, such as ethical reasoning, professional competence, and decision-making skills among future managers. This study addresses this gap by investigating how AI adoption affects the learning behaviors, moral judgment, and professional readiness of Business Administration and Accountancy students in private higher education institutions in Bulacan City. The study emphasizes the theoretical relevance of AI-mediated decision-making and ethical development for management studies, extending insights beyond the classroom to organizational and managerial contexts. The research applies Kohlberg’s Moral Development Theory, the AI Acceptance in Education Framework, Digital Learning Agency Theory, and the Future-Ready Graduate Framework to explore how AI integration influences ethical reasoning, learning efficiency, and professional competence. A quantitative research design measures the frequency, purpose, and context of AI tool usage and examines its relationship with learning behaviors, moral reasoning, and ethical decision-making. Statistical analyses, including correlation and regression models, identify systematic patterns and variations in AI adoption and ethical judgment, providing evidence of both enhanced efficiency and potential ethical challenges. Findings indicate that students use AI predominantly for drafting, proofreading, and information synthesis. While this improves academic efficiency, it also introduces challenges to ethical reasoning and moral judgment, suggesting that AI adoption can shape decision-making behaviors relevant to managerial contexts. Differences in ethical judgment appear to correlate with the level of AI familiarity, digital literacy, and awareness of ethical standards. These results contribute to management theory by demonstrating how emerging digital tools influence the development of ethical competence, professional decision-making skills, and digital agency, which are critical for future organizational leaders. The study provides a theoretical framework linking AI adoption in educational contexts to managerial decision-making, ethical reasoning, and professional competence. This framework offers insights for management research on technology-mediated decision-making and informs practical strategies for developing future-ready managers capable of ethical and efficient decisionmaking in AI-driven environments. The findings also have implications for organizational training programs, ethical policy development, and management education curricula, underscoring the importance of integrating AI literacy and ethical awareness into professional development.

title_key: personalization and individualization of continuing professional education programs through artificial intelligence|andreeva
title: Personalization and individualization of continuing professional education programs through artificial intelligence
abstract: The article focuses on the analysis of generative artificial intelligence (AI) potential for implementing personalized and individualized approaches in continuing professional education (CPE). The purpose of the study is to substantiate a model for adapting professional development programs to the diverse needs of adult learners using AI technologies. The empirical basis is the program "Neural Networks in Foreign Language Teaching," where AI tools were applied for needs assessment, content adjustment, and development of differentiated tasks. The research novelty lies in the tested model combining learning path differentiation with the development of critical digital literacy. Particular attention is paid to fostering participants' ability to critically evaluate AI-generated content, which corresponds to the AI Competency Framework for Teachers (UNESCO). The results highlight the potential of integrating AI into CPE to enhance personalization opportunities and support teachers' professional growth. The paper offers practical recommendations for designing adaptive educational programs based on AI technologies.

title_key: a challenge based learning experience for teaching industry 5 0 in management engineering education|prieto
title: A Challenge-Based Learning Experience for Teaching Industry 5.0 in Management Engineering Education
abstract: Industry 5.0 demands that engineering graduates develop competencies that integrate technical knowledge with human-centricity, sustainability and resilience. However, engineering education has not always advanced at the same pace, and effective educational designs that operationalise these principles within applied learning contexts remain scarce. This paper presents Innovation Day, a four-hour challenge-based learning experience that operationalises Industry 5.0 principles through an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported cyber–physical logistics challenge in management engineering master’s programmemes. The activity engaged 47 students organised into 14 teams across two master’s degrees at the Universitat Politècnica de València. Students progressively developed and integrated data structuring, QR-based identification, sequencing and storage assignment logic, computer vision and collaborative robotics within a single supervised automation workflow. All 14 teams completed the first three phases, while completion rates reached 71% in Phase 4 and 64% in Phase 5, reflecting the increasing demands of system integration. Results also show that generative AI acted as a pedagogical tool, enabling students with limited programming experience to develop functional Python applications while maintaining human validation and accountability. The experience demonstrates that complex Industry 5.0 scenarios can be translated into manageable, transferable educational activities through phased challenge design, functional validation gates and structured AI-supported learning.

title_key: artificial intelligence in physics education research in two decades a bibliometric study from scopus database|nurjanah
title: Artificial Intelligence in Physics Education Research in Two Decades: A Bibliometric Study from Scopus Database
abstract: There has been a substantial rise in research on utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology in physics education. This study conducts a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of this emerging field, aiming to discern trends, patterns, and future research areas. Using the PRISMA methodology, data were extracted from the Google Scholar and Scopus databases and analyzed with Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. We identified 12 main topic clusters, including chatbot applications and 3D virtual simulations, with significant growth in publications from 2020 to 2023. Key findings focused on pre-trained language models like ChatGPT, revealing strong connections between ChatGPT and topics such as linguistic quality and student perception. Future research areas can include thorough evaluations of AI models' accuracy and quality across various physics topics and educational levels, developing fair and transparent AI-driven assessment systems, and exploring blended learning approaches integrating AI-powered simulations. Encouraging interdisciplinary collaborations and conducting longitudinal studies to assess the long-term impact of AI on learning outcomes are also crucial. The use of Google Scholar and Scopus databases limits our research. Future research could benefit from incorporating other databases, such as Web of Science (WoS), and conducting a systematic literature review for a more nuanced understanding.

title_key: comparing human designed and ai enhanced science lessons a pilot study in k 5 education|senese
title: Comparing Human-Designed and AI-Enhanced Science Lessons: A Pilot Study in K-5 Education
abstract: Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd) is a rapidly growing field, yet concrete applications in early Science Education remain limited.This pilot study investigates the impact and perception of generative AI tools in designing and delivering science lessons in K-5 classrooms, compared to traditional human-designed instruction.The research was conducted in two phases: i) a preliminary survey involving Italian nursery and primary school teachers to assess familiarity and expectations toward educational technologies, and ii) a field intervention comparing six traditional and six AI-assisted science lessons, followed by a second structured questionnaire completed by seven teachers.Results reveal that while traditional teaching remains essential for fostering foundational skills, empathy, and real-world connections, AI/GAI tools can enhance engagement through immersive and adaptive experiences.However, effective integration requires targeted teacher training and mindful implementation.This study highlights the complementary strengths of human and AI-led instruction, advocating for balanced, inclusive, and pedagogically grounded innovation in early STEM education.However, further research is needed to evaluate long-term educational impact and scalability.

title_key: engineering education in the age of ai protecting learning outcomes while teaching responsible use|hamid
title: Engineering Education in the Age of AI: Protecting Learning Outcomes while Teaching Responsible Use
abstract: Malaysian engineering education is now under two pressures at the same time. Accreditation instruments, chiefly the Engineering Accreditation Council's 2024 Programme Accreditation Standard (EAC 2024) and the Malaysian Qualifications Framework (MQF 2024) of the Malaysian Qualifications Agency, expect graduates to show more than technical competence: ethical judgement, teamwork, communication and sustainability awareness now count as outcomes in their own right. Over roughly the same period, generative artificial intelligence has made it possible for a student to hand in competent-looking coursework without doing the reading and reasoning the assignment was meant to require. The risk is concrete. A student can leave a course knowing less than the curriculum intended while the submitted work looks accomplished. We ask what these two shifts mean when read together, and what they imply for teaching and assessment. Drawing on 36 peer-reviewed, openly accessible sources published between 2019 and 2026, together with the EAC 2024 and MQF 2024 standards, we examine five curriculum strategies that recur in the literature: project-based learning (PBL), service-learning through Malaysia's SULAM framework, value-based education, integration of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and communication-skills instruction. We read them as related responses to one problem. Each depends on a process the student has to go through over time, which is harder to bypass than a single artefact handed in at the end, and each builds outcomes that current accreditation treats as central. Most existing studies treat these themes separately, both from each other and from the assessment concerns raised by AI. We propose an integrative reading in which SULAM-linked, SDG-framed PBL projects, assessed with explicit communication criteria and a documented reasoning process, give programmes a workable route to these outcomes that does not rest on trust alone. The paper ends with practical implications for curriculum and assessment design in Malaysian engineering faculties and points out where local evidence on AI-integrated assessment is still thin.
venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science

title_key: evaluating the efficacy of ai generated inquiry based lesson plans in science|kahraman
title: Evaluating the Efficacy of AI-Generated Inquiry-Based Lesson Plans in Science
abstract: This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of artificial intelligence in creating inquiry-based lesson plans for science education in the context of Turkey. An exploratory design was used to achieve this goal. The subject matter of middle school science was treated as a case and ChatGPT was asked to create lesson plans by specifying the objectives and duration of the lessons. Then, the plans were evaluated by the researchers, considering the rubric of the Guidelines for Assessing Inquiry-based Lesson Plans developed by Borda-Carulla and Harmen (2012). The researchers of this study evaluated the lesson plans separately, and the internal consistency coefficient was calculated as 0.83. The results suggest that the artificial intelligence-generated lesson plans were aligned with the course objectives, incorporated real-world contexts, and promoted an inquiry-based learning environment. Despite these strengths, the results of this study also suggest that some areas need to be improved, such as providing structured feedback and fostering curiosity.

title_key: automated benchmarking infrastructure moving toward robust investigations of gen ai in computing education|ali
title: Automated Benchmarking Infrastructure: Moving Toward Robust Investigations of Gen AI in Computing Education
abstract: D uring a 12-week term in 2024, an average of 32 new large language models (LLMs) were released [4].The most powerful LLMs can generate code explanations, improve error messages, generate code itself, and even simulate students [9,10,11,12].While many LLMs are relatively easy to access and use for computing educators through the Web, consider an educator who wants to see how easy it would be for a student to use the latest version of ChatGPT or Gemini to answer their exam questions.They would have to meticulously structure their prompts to pass into the AI tools and then arduously read through the essay-length, AI-generated outputs for each question to determine correctness.And then they would repeat the process for Gemini.This process is repetitive and tedious, especially when considering that 30+ other new LLMs will become available throughout the term.The educator simply does not have the capacity to keep up.In the spirit of computer science (CS) and automating repetitive tasks, we propose using existing AI benchmarking infrastructure to support more efficient evaluations and reliable comparisons of rapidly evolving LLMs. Introduction: What's an AI Benchmark?How accurate is GPT-4o on this dataset of multiple-choice CS1 questions across campuses?What is the F1 score of Google's latest version of Gemini on this collection of select-all-that-apply quizzes from my algorithms class?Is this new model doing any better on all these instructional materials this term compared to last term?Questions like these make up a large part of generative AI's use in educational settings.It makes sense; the natural place to start exploring a new model is to measure its progress on tasks which reflect meaningful capabilities, such as introductory programming skills.Formally, a benchmark is a set of specific, existing tasks to evaluate an AI model's performance [15].Think of it as a standardized assessment, but for models-in this case, LLMs.If an instructor wants to assess their students' proficiency in a given subject, they can give them a standardized test-everyone gets the same questions, the same amount of time, and the same grading scale.At the end of it, they can compare the skill levels of different students, track individual student progress over time, and record performance at a given time.The instructor "benchmarks" their students' performance.

title_key: developing and validating the harmony model a prophetic values based hadith learning approach integrating digital tools to strengthen university students religious tolerance|sumarna
title: Developing and Validating the HARMONY Model: A Prophetic Values-Based Hadith Learning Approach Integrating Digital Tools to Strengthen University Students’ Religious Tolerance
abstract: Religious tolerance in higher education is important amid exclusivist perspectives and limited contextualization of religious learning in Indonesia’s plural society. Hadith instruction in Islamic Religious Education often emphasizes normative-textual understanding while giving insufficient attention to values relevant to interreligious coexistence. This study developed and preliminarily evaluated prophetic-values-based hadith learning model. A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was employed at four Indonesian universities. The qualitative phase involved semi-structured interviews with 16 participants, producing 651 coded statements that informed the HARMONY model (Hadith Analysis and Reflective Meaning for Openness, Nurturing, and Humanity). The model integrates Maktabah Syamilah, the Encyclopedia of the Nine Hadith Imams, and ChatGPT-supported reflective dialogue. AI-generated information was treated as provisional and verified against authoritative hadith sources under lecturer supervision. The quantitative phase involved 140 students in a one-group pretest–posttest design. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t-tests, Cohen’s d, and N-Gain. Expert evaluation indicated high model validity (M = 3.80/4.00). Significant improvements were observed in hadith learning competence (t = 18.42, p < .001, d = 1.56, N-Gain = 0.71) and self-reported religious tolerance (t = 17.16, p < .001, d = 1.45, N-Gain = 0.68), categorized as high and medium, respectively. These findings provide preliminary evidence of favorable short-term changes following implementation. The study supports SDG 4 through inclusive education and SDG 16 through peaceful coexistence. Further research using comparison groups, multiple measurements, and longer observation is recommended to confirm the findings and strengthen evidence of the model’s effectiveness.

title_key: decoding the use of artificial intelligence in programming education a topic modeling analysis|arslantas
title: Decoding the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Programming Education: A Topic Modeling Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Programming education plays a vital role in today's digital world, and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into this field has attracted growing scholarly attention. Considering this increasing interest, this study explores the evolving landscape of AI in programming education by examining temporal developments and shifting research trends. A total of 1186 articles published between 1977 and 2025 and indexed in the Scopus database were analyzed using machine learning‐based semantic topic modeling and descriptive analysis. The results reveal patterns in publication trends over time, key contributing countries, and the distribution of studies across journals and conference proceedings. Topic modeling identified 12 major themes, with the most prominent including “Learning Methods & Teaching Support,” “Programming Errors & Code Learning,” “Programming Courses & Student Performance,” and “ChatGPT in Programming Education.” This study offers a comprehensive overview of the field's development, providing valuable insights for researchers, educators, and policymakers.

title_key: intelligenze artificiali tra etica e diritti uso di chatgpt in un corso sul diritto dautore per bibliotecari|robbio
title: Intelligenze artificiali tra etica e diritti: uso di ChatGPT in un corso sul diritto d’autore per bibliotecari
abstract: This article is based on conversations that took place between me and ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence model created to interact conversationally like a human, in a kind of internal investigation into its own functioning. The topics of the conversations with the chatbot concern aspects of intellectual property and library and information sciences, which the author is familiar with. The protection of works produced by ChatGPT, a topic that confused it, its ambiguous “relationship” with books and literature, or its uncertain and incomplete production of abstracts in the field of library and information sciences, as well as the distracted and unreliable examination on the copyright’s European Directives, were the subject of live-exercises with participants in the online course organized between February and March 2023 by the Editrice Bibliografica “Managing Copyright in Library Services” taught by the author. The proliferation of news and articles on the ChatGPT phenomenon can be frightening for the many ethical implications and the effects on the future impact that such models can have on our lives. It is therefore important to understand their mechanisms, as only with knowledge can we govern what scares us. We humans must govern machines and this requires new skills that librarians must begin to put comptence’s in-basket. If in the last century automation replaced many manual jobs, now with the advent of artificial intelligence models, especially generative ones, intellectual jobs may be at risk. Librarians have always been at the center of change processes, and this now pervasive phenomenon implies a change in the way we organize our ways of learning and building knowledge.
venue: E-LIS Repository (University of Naples Federico II)

title_key: how design thinking can make stem education thrive in the ai era|vieira
title: How design thinking can make STEM education thrive in the AI era
abstract: In a time where ChatGPT enables students of secondary and tertiary levels to create assignments with just a single click, a pertinent question arises: how do we cultivate critical skills and authenticate their work? Design Thinking offers solutions to these challenges. This article explores the impact of Design Thinking in addressing the issues posed by AI and global digitalisation in STEM education, drawing inspiration from the 'Co-Creating Community Connections' exhibition in Adelaide, South Australia.

title_key: a proposal for automated layperson level companion summaries for all scientific dois a zenodo and cern open science initiative|swygert
title: A Proposal for Automated Layperson-Level Companion Summaries for All Scientific DOIs: A Zenodo and CERN Open Science Initiative
abstract: This proposal outlines a transformative upgrade for Zenodo and CERN Open Science: an automated system that generates layperson-level companion summaries, audio explanations, narration scripts, and optional video explainers for every scientific DOI. The system uses controlled, fidelity-checked LLMs to translate technical papers into accessible educational formats without compromising scientific rigor. By integrating text, audio, and video generation directly on Zenodo’s platform, this initiative turns Zenodo into a global open-university hub—expanding comprehension, reducing scientific inequality, and empowering students, teachers, and lifelong learners worldwide. The proposal includes architecture, safeguards, implementation roadmap, and examples demonstrating how the system enhances understanding while maintaining academic integrity.

title_key: ai enhanced quality of multimodal physics word problems in authentic contexts using the p magic app|hwang
title: AI-Enhanced Quality of Multimodal Physics Word Problems in Authentic Contexts Using the P-MAGIC App
abstract: This study aimed to develop an app called Physics Multimodal Authentic Generated Interactive Content Problem (P-MAGIC) to gather authentic contextual information by using object recognition and real-time sensors to help students learn the principles of centripetal acceleration in Physics. We implemented an instructional-based prompt generator that adjusts the difficulty level of problems in three levels, with the questions themselves being generated by the Generative Pre-trained version 4o (GPT-4o) model. Furthermore, to evaluate our app, we assessed the quality of the generated questions using automatic and human evaluations. The automatic evaluation demonstrated that the questions were relevant, easy to understand, and diverse. Additionally, feedback from teachers showed high ratings for relevance, completeness, and concept accuracy. Interestingly, problems incorporating both text and images, followed by text, images, and graphs, outperformed those that were based on text and graphs or text and tables. This highlights the positive impact of visual elements on conceptual understanding and student engagement. Furthermore, the strong correlation between automatic and human evaluations indicates that automated assessments can reliably reflect human judgement, making them a scalable tool for evaluations. By providing teachers with the tools to create personalized and context-rich problems in a variety of formats could potentially transform physics education.

title_key: modelo geoia m para la mediacion del razonamiento matematico en calculo universitario con inteligencia artificial generativa y geogebra|montenegro
title: MODELO GEOIA-M PARA LA MEDIACIÓN DEL RAZONAMIENTO MATEMÁTICO EN CÁLCULO UNIVERSITARIO CON INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL GENERATIVA Y GEOGEBRA
abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into university calculus teaching has advanced rapidly, yet many observed practices remain instrumental and answer-oriented, which encourages students to delegate their reasoning to the tool. This theoretical-methodological paper proposes and grounds the GeoIA-M Model, a didactic architecture for mediating mathematical reasoning in differential and integral calculus courses, in which generative AI acts as an interlocutor that problematizes and GeoGebra as an environment for exploration, representation and validation. Drawing on a narrative and critical review of recent literature and on the analysis of calculus tasks, the model is organized into five dimensions: exploration, visualization, argumentation, metacognition and ethical reflection and seven implementation phases, placing student reasoning at the center of the process. Two university calculus examples are developed, on optimization with derivatives and on the definite integral and accumulation, including dynamic construction protocols, Socratic querying prompts and process-oriented assessment criteria. The main contribution is an initial didactic architecture to guide classroom practices and teacher education in university Mathematics Education, open to subsequent empirical validation.
venue: Cuadernos de Investigación y Formación en Educación Matemática

title_key: from restricting to integrating ai a university wide strategy for digitalization and ai in engineering education|broberg
title: From restricting to integrating AI: a university-wide strategy for digitalization and AI in engineering education
abstract: Many engineering programs initially responded to generative AI by trying to restrict student use, mainly to protect academic integrity, while work life demands AI-literate graduates across all disciplines and regulation such as the EU AI Act raises requirements for transparency, safety and accountability. Against this backdrop, Chalmers University of Technology has developed a university-wide Strategy for Digitalization and AI in Education that shifts focus from blocking AI to systematically integrating digitalization and AI into curricula, learning processes, pedagogy, faculty competence, support services and the digital infrastructure. A central feature is a three-level learning-outcome model (“for all, for many, for some”) that guarantees basic digital and AI literacy for every student, offers discipline-specific deepening for many, and provides advanced expertise for some in specialized master’s programs. Pedagogical principles stress that digital tools and AI should support rather than replace student thinking and effort, and that assessment must remain valid and fair in an AI-rich environment. The strategy, grounded in current-state and SWOT analyses, is implemented through Chalmers’ matrix governance with program-level ownership, shared guidelines, coordinated faculty development, and investments in infrastructure. The paper presents the strategy as a roadmap for aligning pedagogy, regulation and labor-market demand, and discusses implications for curriculum design, assessment and faculty competence.
authors: ["Niklas Broberg", "Jim Brouzoulis", "Mikael Enelund", "Fia Christina B\u00f6rjesson", "Victoria Granstr\u00f6m", "Aidin Fanni", "Amanda \u00d6berg", "Knut \u00c5kesson"]

title_key: vibe coding as a teaching competency in the use of artificial intelligence for medical education a scoping review|garcia
title: Vibe-coding as a Teaching Competency in the Use of Artificial Intelligence for Medical Education: A Scoping Review
abstract: Introduction: The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence has given rise to vibe-coding, a paradigm that allows educators without technical backgrounds to develop software using natural language. This advancement necessitates redefining the teaching competencies required to transition from users to creators of educational tools. Methods: A scoping review of the literature was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Studies retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus databases addressing the use of vibe-coding by educators in higher and medical education were included. After the selection process, four publications from 2025 were included. A deductive reflexive thematic analysis was applied to classify findings according to the TPACK model dimensions (Technological, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge). Results: Qualitative analysis reveals a reconfiguration of Technological Knowledge (TK), which dissociates from programming syntax to focus on structuring prompts and iterative dialogue with AI. The emergence of the “clinician-developer” role was identified, where Content Knowledge (CK) acts as an indispensable auditing mechanism to validate clinical accuracy and prevent hallucinations in generated algorithms. Technological-Pedagogical Knowledge (TPK) enabled educators to deconstruct complex logic into sequential steps to design simulators and personalized tools. Conclusions: Preliminary evidence suggests that vibe-coding democratizes educational software development, allowing educators to materialize complex pedagogical strategies without external technical dependence. This competency appears to demand robust disciplinary mastery to guarantee the safety and quality of the created resources. It is recommended to foster training in this emerging competency and conduct future empirical studies to evaluate the impact of these tools on student learning and teacher cognitive load.

title_key: haiku anagram generation using ai synthesising poetic isomers through metaphor driven prompt engineering educational transformation 002|isao
title: Haiku Anagram Generation Using AI: Synthesising Poetic Isomers Through Metaphor-Driven Prompt Engineering (Educational Transformation 002)
abstract: Description (English) Overview This paper presents a novel approach to Japanese haiku anagram generation by extending a three-fold metaphorical framework—quantum mechanics, crystal-growth theory, and organic chemistry—to guide large language models (LLMs) in generating semantically independent new haikus from the identical 17 syllables (morae) of existing haikus. Key Findings: 1. Isomorphic Generation Success: We successfully demonstrate the generation of semantically and aesthetically independent alternative haikus from identical molecular formulae (17-syllable inventories), treating haiku syllables as organic isomers—compounds with identical atomic composition but radically different properties and meanings. 2. Discovery of Poetic Steganography: Haiku anagrams uniquely exhibit a "dual-plaintext structure," where both the original and generated haikus function as independently meaningful poems. This property—unknown in classical anagram theory—constitutes a new form of poetic steganography with high plausible deniability. 3. Metaphor-Driven Cognitive Amplification: By deliberately invoking organic chemistry terminology (structural isomers, enantiomers, racemic mixtures) in prompt design, we observe a quantifiable improvement in token efficiency and aesthetic coherence, demonstrating that humanistic metaphors can systematically redirect LLM outputs toward higher-order creative goals without algorithmic modification. Background & Context The author is a molecular biologist (specialising in RNA) developing liberal arts curricula for first-year undergraduates at the University of Tokyo. This research emerged not from AI expertise but from classroom practice—a workshop inspired by physicist Terahiko Terada's 1922 essay "Chawan no Yu" (A Lesson from a Tea Cup), which advocates connecting scientific and humanistic knowledge through metaphor. Previous work (Educational Transformation 001) applied quantum and crystallisation metaphors to English anagrams with success. However, when adapted to Japanese haikus, the dual-metaphor framework proved insufficient to capture haiku-specific constraints (5-7-5 syllable structure, kire or caesura, yohaku or poetic silence, seasonal reference). The addition of organic chemistry isomerism as a third metaphor resolved these limitations entirely. Methodological Innovation We introduce: - Three-tiered metaphor protocol: Quantum superposition (possibility-space management) → Crystal nucleation (hierarchical structure-building) → Isomeric transformation (semantic distance calibration) - Two-stage synthesis strategy: Molecular-level (preserving ligatures like chiyo as single morae) and thermal decomposition (atomic-level when molecular synthesis reaches impasse) - Five-axis aesthetic evaluation: Meaningfulness (0.30), kire (0.20), yohaku (0.20), tension with original (0.15), defamiliarisation (0.15) - Isomer taxonomy for poetry: 11 isomer-type classifications mapping to increasingly distant poetic transformations (from renzoku isomer to meso-structure) Practical Outcomes From a pedagogical standpoint, this framework enables students (regardless of domain expertise) to experience how metaphor functions as a cognitive technology—not merely literary decoration but a systematic tool for amplifying AI reasoning capacity. The protocol is fully reproducible and available as a prompt template compatible with any LLM. Broader Significance This work occupies the intersection of three disciplines: 1. Constrained literature (Oulipo aesthetics): How AI pursues poetic freedom within human-designed, absolute constraints (17 syllables) 2. Computational creativity: Using AI as a "mirror" that visualises the structure of human aesthetic intuition, rather than as an automated content generator 3. title_key: information literacy in research training in virtual postgraduate programs|rodriguez
title: Information literacy in research training in virtual postgraduate programs
abstract: Information literacy has become an important component of research training at the postgraduate level, as is the case in online master’s programs in Colombia. Currently, this education is being affected by the saturation of digital platforms and tools used excessively and without control by students, impacting the development of their research work and the resulting academic output. The problem is exacerbated when master’s students rely solely on digital resources for writing their texts, with emerging technologies like generative artificial intelligence becoming their primary assistant, thus neglecting their independent and scientifically rigorous research. This is reflected in their ability to manage information, encountering difficulties in search strategies, selecting academic sources, and validating consulted data. This study aims to explore the role of information literacy in the use of digital resources within postgraduate research processes. The study employed a quantitative, descriptive approach, supported by online questionnaires administered to 100 faculty members of the research component of the online master’s programs at the Minuto de Dios University Corporation (UNIMINUTO). This allowed for the identification of different student practices regarding information management in digital media. The results show frequent use of tools such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) for information retrieval, but also limitations in the proper handling of content, critical analysis, and the identification of validity criteria for selecting theoretical data. Consequences associated with the unregulated use of artificial intelligence were also identified, such as a lack of information filters, a lack of awareness of standards for written work, and the delegation of academic processes to algorithmic systems. The conclusions indicate that access to information does not guarantee research quality; therefore, it is necessary to strengthen information literacy skills focused on analytical and critical thinking, intellectual autonomy, and the ethical use of information in online master’s programs.

title_key: civil engineering education artificial intelligence in transforming traditional learning into intelligent and industry ready education|kapatel
title: Civil Engineering Education: Artificial Intelligence in Transforming Traditional Learning into Intelligent and Industry-Ready Education
abstract: Civil engineering education is undergoing a fundamental transformation as artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly influences both engineering practice and higher education. Traditional classroom-based approaches remain effective for establishing fundamental engineering knowledge; however, they often have limitations in explaining complex, nonlinear, data-intensive, and field-oriented problems involving structural behaviour, geotechnical uncertainty, transportation systems, environmental processes, infrastructure deterioration, Building Information Modelling (BIM), and construction management. The rapid development of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, generative artificial intelligence, intelligent tutoring systems, and digital twins provides new opportunities to overcome these limitations. This review critically examines the emerging role of AI in civil engineering education and proposes an integrated framework linking AI technologies with civil engineering subjects, pedagogical strategies, experiential learning, and industry-oriented competencies. The review synthesizes research concerning AI-assisted structural analysis and health monitoring, geotechnical engineering, transportation and traffic management, environmental engineering, BIM, construction management, infrastructure inspection, risk assessment, and smart-city applications. Particular attention is given to how AI can transform conventional teaching through personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, virtual experimentation, automated assessment, computer-vision-based laboratory activities, predictive modelling, simulation, digital twins, and generative AI-assisted problem solving. Existing evidence indicates that AI can improve student engagement, problem-solving, visualization, feedback, and exposure to real engineering datasets. However, significant challenges remain, including data availability, model reliability, explainability, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, cybersecurity, faculty preparedness, unequal access to technology, and the risk of excessive dependence on AI-generated solutions. The review identifies a critical research gap: existing studies predominantly investigate either AI applications in civil engineering practice or AI applications in education, with limited integration of the two perspectives into a unified civil engineering education framework. Accordingly, this paper proposes an AI-Civil Engineering Education Integration Framework (AI-CEEIF) that connects engineering knowledge, AI literacy, experiential learning, human–AI collaboration, ethical reasoning, and professional competency. The proposed framework provides a basis for curriculum development, teaching innovation, faculty training, assessment redesign, and future empirical research aimed at preparing civil engineering graduates for increasingly intelligent and data-driven infrastructure systems.

title_key: effectiveness of ai assisted game based learning on science learning outcomes intrinsic motivation cognitive load and learning behavior|chen
title: Effectiveness of AI-assisted game-based learning on science learning outcomes, intrinsic motivation, cognitive load, and learning behavior
abstract: This study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of using AI-assisted game-based learning on science learning outcomes, intrinsic motivation, cognitive load, and learning behavior. A total of 202 seventh graders were recruited and randomly assigned to the following three groups: (1) Game only (N = 70), (2) GameGPT (N = 63), and (3) GameGPT_examples (N = 69). The experimental groups received game-based learning with the assistance of ChatGPT with or without examples, while the control group received only game-based learning. The results showed that students in the GameGPT_examples group significantly outperformed those in the Game only group. Students in the GameGPT and GameGPT_examples groups reported significantly higher perceived competence than those in the Game only group. Furthermore, students in the Game only group reported a greater mental burden than those in the GameGPT_examples and GameGPT groups. The findings from learning behavioral analytics and interviews suggest that AI-assisted game-based learning can enhance students' intrinsic motivation, reduce cognitive load, and promote effective learning behavior in science learning. This study has important implications for the design and implementation of AI in game-based learning environments that aim to improve students' learning outcomes and motivation.

title_key: vibe coding dengan paradigma baru pengembangan perangkat lunak berbasis kecerdasan buatan dan implikasinya terhadap produktivitas dan kualitas kode|yuwono
title: Vibe Coding dengan Paradigma Baru Pengembangan Perangkat Lunak Berbasis Kecerdasan Buatan dan Implikasinya terhadap Produktivitas dan Kualitas Kode
abstract: Vibe coding is a software development approach that intensively leverages Large Language Models (LLMs), where developers act as directors and validators rather than direct code writers. This study aims to: (1) characterize vibe coding scientifically, (2) measure its impact on productivity and code quality, (3) identify associated risks, and (4) formulate practical adoption recommendations. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of 47 publications from Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ACM DL (2021–2025) was conducted, combined with an eight-week controlled experiment on two homogeneous groups of fi-nal-year Informatics Engineering students (control n=30, experimental n=30; Mann-Whitney U=427, p=0.83). Results showed the vibe coding group completed an average of 8.3 features (SD=1.2) vs. 5.4 features (SD=0.9) in the conventional group, a statistically significant difference (t(58)=10.47, p<0.001, Cohen’s d=2.70). However, the vibe coding group exhibited a significantly higher bug rate (5.1 bugs/100 LOC vs. 3.8 bugs/100 LOC; t(58)=3.84, p<0.001) and lower self-understood code pro-ficiency (5.9 vs. 8.4 out of 10; t(58)=-9.12, p<0.001). The study concludes that vibe coding effectively increases short-term productivity but risks technical skill erosion and hidden technical debt without rigorous software engineering practices.

title_key: beyond policing ai reflections on teaching assessment and pedagogy in social science education|aborass
title: Beyond policing AI: reflections on teaching, assessment, and pedagogy in social science education
abstract: AI has permeated almost every aspect of our lives. What began as a limited experimental tool has rapidly evolved into a powerful technology, seamlessly woven into our daily routines. Its expansion is not only swift but also reshapes our reality, raising profound questions about the role of the human, the nature of originality, and the boundaries of creativity (Hassan & Kumar, 2024).In academia, AI has become integral to the landscape of research and teaching, shaping much of academic practice. It is present in scientific writing, in the daily workflow, in supporting student assessment, and even in managing routine administrative tasks. Students, for their part, increasingly rely on it for learning, planning assignments, and meeting academic requirements.Recent findings consistently show that AI is becoming an embedded component of students' higher education learning. The 2025 HEPI Student Generative AI Survey reveals a sharp rise in adoption: nearly all students now use AI in some form, compared with only 66% in 2024. Most rely on AI to clarify concepts, summarize articles, and generate research ideas, and around 18% reported incorporating AI-generated text directly into their assignments. Students frequently note that AI saves them time and improves their work. At the same time, many fear of being accused of academic misconduct and are concerned that AI may produce inaccurate or biased results. Women report higher levels of concern, whereas men, as well as students from higher socioeconomic backgrounds and those studying STEM subjects, express greater enthusiasm with the use of AI in academia (Freeman, 2025). Similar findings have emerged in additional studies (Mazaheriyan & Nourbakhsh, 2025;Ravšeljet al., 2025;Vieriu, & Petrea, 2025), reinforcing the understanding that AI is a widespread global phenomenon actively reshaping both the learning experience and the pedagogical landscape Alongside the rapid increase in students' use of AI, a range of dilemmas has emerged within the academic sphere. Beyond issues of academic integrity, such as uncredited use of AIgenerated outputs or the blurring of boundaries between legitimate assistance and fully AIproduced work, concerns have also been raised about potential harm to core learning skills, including critical thinking, creativity, and even the ability to read and write independently.Additional dilemmas, such as exposure to inaccurate or biased information, widening gender and socioeconomic gaps, and how to assess student work, further underscore the complexity this new technology introduces (Lowe, 2024).As a new faculty member, I am sometimes struck by the intensity of the dilemmas and the extent to which the discourse around AI has come to dominate academic conversations. I have received a steady stream of emails from the university: guidelines on acceptable uses of AI, formal requirements for courses, and best practice statements on academic integrity that faculty are expected to embed in their syllabi. Many of these documents lack clarity, some of their recommendations are difficult to implement in practice, and most are subject to frequent revisions. Interviews with higher education leaders across the globe express the same preoccupation with students' use of AI and level of oversight required.My experience is also shaped by everyday conversations with colleagues, many of whom describe a persistent sense of uncertainty regarding the assessment of student work. Some have shifted from written assignments to closed-book exams in an effort to maintain academic integrity, whether as an individual choice or as part of a broader departmental or institutional approach. Others fear that AI may erode foundational skills such as critical and analytical skills and the ability to formulate coherent arguments.Unlike the prevailing anxieties voiced by institutions and colleagues, however, I do not feel threatened by it -certainly not within the social sciences. Rather, I see AI as a productive challenge: an opportunity to rethink the very nature of teaching and to revisit the foundational goals of student training. From my perspective, the current debate primarily exposes what we have neglected long before the advent of AI-a clear articulation of what our teaching is meant to accomplish. The central question is not how to police the use of AI, but whether we expect students merely to memorize content and produce written assignments or aim to foster deeper competencies. There appears to be a broad consensus that higher education aims to develop skills rather than merely transmit knowledge. If so, AI cannot threaten the core of social science education, as it is fundamentally incapable of replacing the acquisition and honing of skills grounded in human interaction, dialogue, and collective learning spaces, such as critical thinking, reflexivity, and leadership.Informed by this understanding, I find myself questioning how I can teach social science courses to groups of 120 students. Even when these are introductory or research method classes, teaching at such a scale fundamentally undermines the stated goal of skill development, AI or no AI. It is difficult-if not impossible-to cultivate critical thinking, thoughtful discussion, and analytical practice in mass classrooms where opportunities for meaningful interaction are limited.The ongoing debate surrounding student assessment in the age of AI further highlights the gap between our educational aims and prevailing practices. As we have seen, one of the prominent concerns in that age is with assessment. But are the exam or assignment grade the true product of the learning process? Can they genuinely reflect the capacities of those being trained to become social science professionals? Does the fear of compromised "authenticity" in student work not obscure a deeper question about the very purpose of assessment?The current preoccupation with the credibility of submitted assignments and test revives the perennial question: Who is responsible for academic integrity? At times, universities appear eager to assume total responsibility by setting rules and monitoring compliance, yet even the most stringent measures prove largely unworkable. Many institutions have come to recognize that preventing the use of AI is infeasible, opting instead for permitting its use under specified conditions and requiring formal declarations. However, such policies are rarely enforceable and do little to address the core issue, so that responsibility for AI use-and for academic integrity-ultimately remains with the students. I believe the solution lies in a decisive shift toward very small learning groups. Such a move is not intended merely to prevent AI from undermining the quality or integrity of education, but first and foremost to ensure that we are genuinely cultivating the skills we expect social science students to develop. A systematic transition to small-group teachingincluding in introductory and research methods courses-would enable the use of a wide range of pedagogical practices that foster deep learning: open dialogical spaces in which every voice can be heard, collaborative teamwork, the analysis of complex social situations, case-based learning, peer teaching practices, and individual and collective reflective exercises. Within small groups, learning processes can be built around dialogue, shared inquiry, and the coconstruction of meaning, rather than the passive consumption of information. A classic meta-analysis has demonstrated that small-group learning produces superior outcomes in higher education, both in academic achievement and in the development of cognitive and social skills (Springer et al., 1999). Moreover, small-group learning constitutes a central component of highimpact educational practices, which aim to promote meaningful learning, deep skill development, and personal and social responsibility as students engage with complex societal issues (Kuh, 2008).The shift to small also requires a transformation in modes of instruction, including preparing instructors to teach in ways that allow students to lead portions of the class, present insights, pose questions, and practice skills in real time. In such settings, learning becomes genuinely interactive-not as a technological simulation, but as a human process that unfolds within the classroom. In this context, as a faculty member, I am often encouraged to integrate "engagement-enhancing" technological tools, such as Wooclap and similar platforms, to maximize student participation and speak in a language familiar to them. Yet in my experience, these tools tend to create only a brief departure from an otherwise unidirectional lecture. They do not replace authentic interaction, they do not deepen learning, and at times even produce a sense of paternalism-as if the instructor's role were to "entertain" or "occupy" students rather than to lead a meaningful pedagogical process. Our responsibility is not to amuse our students but to create a space that enables the practice and development of skills; the students' responsibility, in turn, is to participate actively in the learning process.Within this context, I find it essential to place interdisciplinary thinking at the center of small-group teaching-not only at the level of course content, but also in terms of the group composition and the structure of instruction. One can imagine models in which a small group is composed of students from different social science departments, and the course is co-taught by two instructors from distinct disciplines who actively model interdisciplinary dialogue: points of disagreement, areas of overlap, and moments of complementarity. Such models represent not merely pedagogical but a reflection of the professional reality in which social science graduates ultimately operate, where fields are rarely isolated, and meaningful work is almost always carried out through sustained interdisciplinary collaboration.For example, I would like to see a course such as Developmental Psychology for Social Work taught jointly to students of social work, education, psychology, and sociology. This form of learning enables students to examine how the same theoretical knowledge is applied across different professional contexts: how developmental psychology informs the field practice of a social worker, the pedagogical perspective of an educator, the clinical framing of a psychologist, or the societal analysis of a sociologist.While such models already exist in some universities, they are often treated as exceptions, requiring special approvals, dedicated resources, and deviations from standard curricula. I argue for a reversed logic: interdisciplinary small-group teaching should become the norm. If we are truly committed to preparing graduates to engage with complex social realities, we must intentionally design interdisciplinary learning frameworks not as marginal elective offerings, but as an integral component of the core training. Small groups are not only a foundation for deeper interaction, but also a way to move beyond the limitations of traditional assessment practices. Particularly in large courses, exams and written assignments fail to reveal the full potential of many students. Having studied social sciences in a second language -often as the only minority student in the classroom -I frequently struggled to express my abilities. In mass lectures, I rarely spoke, and for many years, I felt a gap between my true skills and their evaluation.In small-group settings, by contrast, marginalized students can be seen, heard, and fully exercise their abilities, while instructors are better able to identify skills that do not easily surface through conventional assessment. Small groups make it possible to see everyone, not only the confident, dominant, and fluent students. They allow instructors to offer close guidance, recognize potential, offer support, and actively work to reduce gaps. In this sense, rather than allowing AI to deepen existing inequalities, small-group learning creates a space that strengthens equity. This perspective resonates with critical pedagogical traditions in higher education, which emphasize visibility, voice, and relational engagement as essential not only for meaningful learning, but also for fostering a more inclusive and just academic environment for marginalized students (hooks, 2014).Small-group learning also enables richer and more flexible forms of assessment: longitudinal evaluation, assessment of participation, scaffolded writing processes, close mentoring, and greater attention to effort and learning processes rather than to final products. These forms of evaluation also alleviate concerns about plagiarism or inappropriate uses of AI.Indeed, AI can be intentionally integrated into the learning process-not as a substitute for learning, but as a point of departure. Students can bring AI-generated texts into the classroom, and analyze, critique, and rebuild them. Through this process, they learn not only disciplinary content, but also how AI operates within social systems, reproduces power relations, and transforms modes of knowledge production-questions that lie at the very heart of the social

title_key: the instructional justification of formal concept entry in science education a concept genesis framework|sivasubramanian
title: The instructional justification of formal concept entry in science education: a concept genesis framework
abstract: Science education seeks not only to expand learners' knowledge but also to develop scientific ways of explaining natural phenomena. This requires more than transmitting disciplinary information. Learners must recognise why scientific concepts become necessary, how they extend or revise existing explanations, and under what conditions they provide meaningful accounts of the physical world. The educational challenge therefore concerns not only which concepts should be taught, but also the instructional reasoning surrounding their introduction.Science education research has generated substantial knowledge through conceptual change, inquiry-based learning, model-based instruction, learning progressions, productive preparation, and related traditions. These approaches have shown the importance of engaging prior ideas, recognising explanatory limitations, refining representations, and applying knowledge across contexts. Yet one decision connecting many of these processes often remains implicit: the introduction of formal scientific concepts (Duit and Treagust, 2012;Méheut and Psillos, 2004;Steenhof et al., 2020;Minner et al., 2010;Campbell et al., 2015).In this article, formal concept entry refers to the point at which a scientific construct is presented in an explicit disciplinary form, for example as a named concept or definition, symbolic or mathematical representation, law, model, or related formal structure. Such constructs frequently enter instruction through curricular sequence, textbook organisation, or teaching convention. These arrangements may be appropriate, but the educational justification for formal concept entry is seldom examined directly: not whether the construct belongs in the curriculum, but whether its formal presentation is coordinated with the explanatory work Commented [S[1]: 'U' was missing in '.edu'. Now that is included learners are expected to perform. This issue has renewed practical importance as learners increasingly encounter completed definitions, derivations, simulations, and explanations through digital platforms and generative artificial intelligence before instruction has established their explanatory significance. Greater access to formal scientific information does not itself establish when a construct becomes meaningful within learners' developing understanding (Kumar et al., 2026). This Opinion therefore argues that formal concept entry deserves explicit consideration as an instructional decision. The central question is not whether formal scientific concepts should be introduced early or late, but whether their introduction is instructionally justified by the explanatory work learners are expected to perform.To support reflection on this question, I propose the Concept Genesis Framework (CGF). CGF is an instructor-facing conceptual architecture for examining how formal scientific concepts are prepared, introduced, interpreted, and integrated within learning. It neither replaces established educational theories nor prescribes a universal teaching sequence. Its contribution is to provide a coherent language for considering the instructional justification of formal concept entry.CGF does not arise from a single theory of learning. Its design draws on several established traditions that converge on a common instructional concern: learners interpret new scientific ideas through prior understanding, may need to recognise limitations in existing explanations, and require representational and explanatory support to integrate new disciplinary constructs.Conceptual-change scholarship provides one foundation through its attention to existing conceptions, explanatory inadequacy, and the restructuring of understanding (Strike and Posner, 1982;Duit and Treagust, 2012). Nersessian (1989) adds a representational perspective by emphasising that scientific understanding involves the construction and coordination of conceptual and mathematical representations rather than the reception of completed definitions alone. Inquiry and teaching-learning sequence research further situate such conceptual development within deliberately organised instructional activity (Sandoval and Reiser, 2004;Méheut and Psillos, 2004).CGF does not depend on a single philosophical doctrine. Its orientation is epistemic and instructional: scientific concepts are treated as disciplinary resources for explanation, representation, and prediction rather than as isolated verbal or symbolic entities.
